findings.message: CreateCredential is called without first deleting the existing credential. Per the gptscript pattern ('The only way to update a credential is to delete the existing one and recreate it.' — modelprovider.go:299), calling CreateCredential when a credential already exists will fail. This means any catalog update that keeps at least one token (including edits that don't change the URL at all) will error on the second and all subsequent calls. The fix is to delete the existing credential before creating the new one when existingCred.Env is non-empty and newTokens is non-empty.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The codebase consistently documents 'The only way to update a credential is to delete the existing one and recreate it' (modelprovider.go:294, authprovider.go:159, filescannerprovider.go:206, mcp.go:1919, systemmcpserver.go:160), and all those sites delete before calling CreateCredential. The new mcpcatalogs.go Update handler calls CreateCredential directly when newTokens is non-empty, without first deleting the existing credential. This will fail on any second update that retains at least one token.
findings.severity_justification: Any admin update to a catalog that already has tokens stored will error on the second call, making token-based private repo catalogs impossible to update after the first save.
findings.category_justification: The code will produce an error at runtime due to violating the gptscript credential API contract (create fails if credential already exists), breaking the core update flow.

findings.message: When the `*` sentinel is received for a URL, the backend looks up `existingCred.Env[u]` where `u` is the new URL. If the URL was renamed (old URL had a token, new URL does not), the lookup returns empty and the token is silently dropped. The frontend at McpServerGitSync.svelte:163-170 sends `{newURL: '*'}` and deletes the old URL key, expecting the backend to transfer the token — but the backend has no transfer logic. The comment 'transferred from a renamed one' is incorrect; this case is not implemented.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified by tracing the rename flow: frontend sends {newURL: '*'} (after deleting old URL key), but backend only looks up existingCred.Env[newURL] which doesn't exist (stored under old URL key). The preservation loop skips newURL because it was mentioned in SourceURLCredentials. Token is silently dropped. The comment 'transferred from a renamed one' is factually wrong — no such logic exists.
findings.severity_justification: Causes silent token loss when an admin renames a private repo URL, breaking sync for that catalog until the token is manually re-entered. Functional data loss but not catastrophic — user can recover by re-entering the token.
findings.category_justification: Logic error: the '*' sentinel for a URL rename doesn't transfer the token, contrary to the comment claiming it does.

findings.message: catalog.Spec.SourceURLs is persisted via req.Update() before the credential is saved. If CreateCredential subsequently fails (including due to the 'already exists' bug), the catalog is left in an inconsistent state: its URLs are updated but the corresponding tokens are not stored or updated. Future syncs for URLs that require a token will fail silently. The credential write should either be attempted before the catalog update or the entire operation should be made atomic (delete old credential, update catalog, create new credential, with rollback on failure).
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: req.Update(&catalog) is called at line 197, persisting SourceURLs, before CreateCredential at line 203. If CreateCredential fails (including due to the 'already exists' bug identified separately), the catalog has updated URLs but no corresponding tokens, leaving private-repo URLs in a broken sync state. The ordering issue is real and correctible by swapping the two operations.
findings.severity_justification: Creates an inconsistency window where catalog URLs are updated but tokens are not, causing private repo syncs to fail silently. Severity is medium rather than high because the failure is recoverable (user can retry), and the window only matters if the credential store fails independently, which is uncommon — though exacerbated by the 'already exists' bug.
findings.category_justification: Concerns the ordering of two writes to separate stores without rollback, leaving the system in an inconsistent state if the second write fails.

findings.message: revealCatalogCredential is called once per sourceURL inside the sync loop, but each call fetches the exact same single credential (same context name + tool name). For a catalog with N source URLs this results in N redundant RPCs to the gptscript daemon. The credential should be fetched once before the loop and the relevant key extracted per sourceURL.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: revealCatalogCredential always calls h.gptClient.RevealCredential with the same (catalogName, CatalogCredentialToolName) arguments regardless of sourceURL. The sourceURL parameter is only used to index into cred.Env after the fetch. For N source URLs, N identical RPCs are made where 1 would suffice.
findings.severity_justification: The redundant RPCs are to the local gptscript daemon, not a remote service, and catalogs typically have few source URLs. Syncs run hourly. The inefficiency is real but has negligible practical impact.
findings.category_justification: Redundant RPCs in a loop where a single fetch outside the loop would suffice.

findings.message: manifest.SourceURLs entries are normalized (scheme-less strings like 'github.com/org/repo' get 'https://' prepended), but the keys of manifest.SourceURLCredentials are not normalized. If a client sends a scheme-less URL as a credential key, it will not match any entry in activeURLs (which was built from the normalized SourceURLs), so the token is silently discarded rather than stored.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: manifest.SourceURLs entries are normalized to 'https://' in-place, so activeURLs contains normalized keys. But manifest.SourceURLCredentials keys are never normalized. A user typing a scheme-less URL while also entering a token will have their credential key not match any activeURLs entry, silently discarding the token.
findings.severity_justification: Requires a user to type a scheme-less URL and provide a token simultaneously in the same save operation — an uncommon input. The token loss is discoverable (no '*' shown on next load) and the user can retry. No security or data integrity risk beyond requiring a re-entry.
findings.category_justification: Asymmetric normalization between SourceURLs and SourceURLCredentials keys causes a silent mismatch that drops tokens.

findings.message: resolveToken compares catalogURL to the hardcoded defaultCatalogURL string 'https://github.com/obot-platform/mcp-catalog' with exact equality. If the operator stores the default catalog URL with a .git suffix ('https://github.com/obot-platform/mcp-catalog.git'), the comparison fails and GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN is not used as the fallback token. The function should strip the .git suffix before comparing, or compare after normalizing via parseGitURL's cloneURL output.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: resolveToken(token, catalogURL) uses the original catalogURL (may include .git) against the hardcoded constant 'https://github.com/obot-platform/mcp-catalog' (no .git). If the operator configures the default catalog URL with .git suffix, the exact-equality check fails and GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN is not returned. The PR itself adds .git suffix support throughout, making this an inconsistency in the new code.
findings.severity_justification: Only affects the GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN fallback for the obot-platform catalog, which is a public repo — the token is for rate-limiting only. Operators who omit .git are unaffected. No security or functional breakage, just potential rate-limiting without the token.
findings.category_justification: Inconsistency in URL normalization: .git suffix is stripped for clone URL construction but not for the defaultCatalogURL equality check in resolveToken.

findings.message: checkGitHubRepoSize is called from readGitCatalog with effectiveToken (already fully resolved via resolveToken), but then calls resolveToken again internally with a newly constructed URL. This double-resolution is harmless when effectiveToken is non-empty (resolveToken returns it unchanged), but is misleading: the function signature implies it receives a raw token but receives a pre-resolved one, creating confusion about which layer is responsible for token resolution.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: readGitCatalog resolves effectiveToken via resolveToken(token, catalogURL), then passes effectiveToken to checkGitHubRepoSize which calls resolveToken(effectiveToken, ...) again. The double-resolution is harmless (resolveToken short-circuits when token != "") but the function's doc comment 'Falls back to GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN if no per-URL token is provided' is misleading since it always receives a pre-resolved token.
findings.severity_justification: No actual behavior difference in any code path — purely a misleading interface contract and confusing responsibility layering. A competent reader could be confused about which layer resolves the token.
findings.category_justification: Confusing interface contract where the token parameter and doc comment imply unresolved input, but pre-resolved tokens are always passed, making the internal fallback logic redundant and misleading.

findings.message: sizeLimitedFile.Write atomically adds len(p) bytes to the written counter before deciding whether to reject the write. When the limit is exceeded, the bytes are counted but not written. This over-counting means the guard triggers correctly, but the boundary behavior is that a write which crosses the limit (e.g. 5 MB remaining, 10 MB write attempted) is rejected entirely rather than allowing the 5 MB partial write. While this is stricter than necessary, the actual concern is that once a write adds bytes to the counter and is rejected, those bytes remain counted, permanently making the counter larger than the actual bytes written. In the single-clone-then-discard use case this doesn't matter, but it would matter if the struct were reused.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The technical behavior described is accurate (counter overshoots on rejected writes), but the finding's own conclusion is that this doesn't matter in the single-clone-then-discard use case, which is the only use case in the codebase. The struct is created fresh per readGitCatalog call and is never reused. The hypothetical struct-reuse concern is unsupported by any current code.
findings.severity_justification: Even if considered a concern, the struct is always discarded after one use, making the over-counting permanently irrelevant.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about counter semantics and potential reuse concerns in an implementation detail.

findings.message: When editing a URL and the user leaves the token field empty (no new token entered), the frontend detects the URL was renamed and remaps the sourceURLCredentials key from oldUrl to newUrl with value '*'. However, the backend's `case "*":` handler only preserves a token if existingCred.Env[newUrl] already has a value — which it won't since newUrl is new. The token is silently lost. There is no server-side support for credential key transfer on URL rename; the user must re-enter the token after renaming a URL.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is the same bug as Finding 2, verified against the same code paths: frontend sends {newURL: '*'} (McpServerGitSync.svelte lines 163-170), backend looks up existingCred.Env[newURL] which is empty since the token was stored under oldURL, token silently dropped. The description is factually correct.
findings.severity_justification: Causes silent token loss when an admin renames a private repo URL, requiring manual re-entry of the token before sync works again.
findings.category_justification: Logic error in credential transfer on URL rename — the '*' sentinel doesn't actually transfer the token from old key to new key.

findings.message: The error check `errors.As(err, &notFound)` where `notFound` is `gptscript.ErrNotFound{}` is likely incorrect. `errors.As` requires the second argument to be a pointer to a type that implements the `error` interface. `&gptscript.ErrNotFound{}` is a pointer to a struct, which is valid, but this change from `(*gptscript.ErrNotFound)(nil)` might be unintentional or based on a misunderstanding. It's better to use `var notFound *gptscript.ErrNotFound` to avoid potential issues with how `errors.As` works with non-nil struct pointers.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The pattern errors.As(err, &gptscript.ErrNotFound{}) is the dominant established convention used in 15+ locations across the codebase. The PR change aligns credentials.go with this convention. The finding incorrectly claims this form might be incorrect and suggests reverting to the old pointer-to-nil-pointer form that the rest of the codebase has already moved away from.
findings.severity_justification: Even if taken at face value, both forms work correctly with errors.As given how gptscript.ErrNotFound implements error.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about whether the errors.As call works correctly.

findings.message: When `os.MkdirTemp` fails, the error is returned without being wrapped. This will cause the controller to retry the operation, but the error message will lack context about which operation failed (e.g., creating a temporary directory for a specific catalog URL).
findings.tp_fp_justification: The actual code at line 319-321 already wraps the error: `return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to create temporary directory: %w", err)`. The finding's claim that the error is returned without wrapping is factually wrong.
findings.severity_justification: The claimed issue doesn't exist in the code.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about error message context/wrapping quality.

findings.message: The validation for branch names is incomplete. It checks for `..`, `\`, `:`, and a `-` prefix, but a branch name could still contain characters that are invalid for a git reference, like spaces or other special characters. This could lead to clone failures or other unexpected behavior in `go-git`.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While the validation is technically incomplete, the missing characters (spaces, etc.) cause go-git to fail the clone with a proper error that is already caught and returned. The security-relevant patterns are already blocked (.. for path traversal, : for refspec injection, - prefix for option injection). Only admins can set catalog URLs. The finding doesn't demonstrate a concrete exploitable issue beyond a slightly less friendly error message from go-git.
findings.severity_justification: No security or data integrity risk; worst case is a confusing error message from go-git when an admin types a branch name with unusual characters.
findings.category_justification: The finding is framed as incomplete security validation of user input.

findings.message: The call to `git.CloneContext` uses `limitedFS` for the filesystem but not for the worktree. According to go-git documentation, `git.CloneContext` expects a `billy.Filesystem` for the worktree argument, but `limitedFS` is passed as the `storer` argument's filesystem, not as the worktree filesystem. The call should be `git.CloneContext(ctx, storer, limitedFS, cloneOptions)` to correctly limit the size of the cloned worktree files.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The actual code at line 343 already reads `git.CloneContext(ctx, storer, limitedFS, cloneOptions)` — limitedFS is already passed as the worktree filesystem. The finding's proposed fix is identical to what is already written. The claim that limitedFS is not passed as the worktree argument is factually wrong.
findings.severity_justification: The issue described doesn't exist in the code.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes an incorrect factual claim about what arguments are passed to git.CloneContext.

findings.message: When fetching a raw file catalog from a private source using a token, the token is sent in an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. This is appropriate for many services like GitHub, but it's not a universal standard. Some git hosting services or simple file servers might expect the token in a different header (e.g., `PRIVATE-TOKEN` for GitLab) or as a query parameter. This could cause catalog syncs to fail for some private sources that are not git repositories.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code at lines 181-183 is new to this PR and uses Authorization: Bearer for all non-git URL token authentication. This is factually accurate — Bearer isn't universal and would fail for services requiring PRIVATE-TOKEN or other schemes. The finding identifies a specific limitation in new code.
findings.severity_justification: Only affects non-git raw file sources requiring non-standard auth mechanisms, which is an edge case. Auth failures are visible (HTTP error response), not silent. Bearer covers the vast majority of use cases.
findings.category_justification: The implementation makes an assumption (Bearer is sufficient for all token auth) that may not hold for all raw file source configurations.

findings.message: When a catalog source URL is edited, the logic attempts to transfer an existing credential from the old URL to the new one. However, the check `updatingCatalog.sourceURLCredentials?.[oldUrl] === '*'` will always be false because `updatingCatalog` is a shallow copy of `defaultCatalog`, and the credentials map on `defaultCatalog` is newly created in the `save` function from `catalogToUse`. The credentials map on `catalogToUse` is also always `undefined`. As a result, credentials are never correctly transferred when a URL is renamed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding incorrectly claims updatingCatalog.sourceURLCredentials?.[oldUrl] === '*' is always false. updatingCatalog is a shallow copy of catalogToUse (which is defaultCatalog or a freshly-fetched API response), so updatingCatalog.sourceURLCredentials holds the same reference as the API-populated sourceURLCredentials map containing '*' values. The check works correctly to detect if the old URL had a token.
findings.severity_justification: The finding describes a bug that would cause silent credential loss on URL rename, but the described mechanism is incorrect — the actual frontend code works as intended.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes incorrect claims about JavaScript object reference semantics and data flow.

findings.message: Error handling for `git.CloneContext` is not specific enough. If the clone fails because the repository is too large, it returns a generic "repository is too large" error. However, a clone can fail for many other reasons (e.g., invalid branch, authentication failure, network issues). The error message should be more specific to help users diagnose the problem. For instance, distinguishing between a size limit error and a 'branch not found' error would be more helpful.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code already handles the distinct errRepoTooLarge case and wraps all other clone errors with %w, preserving the full underlying go-git error message. The finding suggests adding more case-specific messages but the current errors are already diagnosable. This is a generic 'improve error messages' suggestion that could apply to any codebase.
findings.severity_justification: No functional regression; errors are already surfaced to the admin via %w wrapping.
findings.category_justification: Suggestion about improving error message specificity for diagnostics.

findings.message: The sizeLimitedFS implementation only caps write operations but does not account for files directly renamed or copied into the directory via methods like Rename or Link, potentially bypassing the size limit enforcement.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While Rename and Link are not overridden in sizeLimitedFS, they cannot introduce untracked new data during a git clone. All data from the remote must go through Create/OpenFile/TempFile + Write, which are all tracked. Rename only moves already-counted data; Link only aliases already-counted data. The 'bypass' scenario is not achievable in the git clone workflow.
findings.severity_justification: Even if taken at face value, the git clone workflow doesn't provide a path for untracked data to enter via Rename or Link.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about potential bypasses of the size enforcement mechanism.

findings.message: The update operation allows tokens to be removed or modified but does not validate the integrity or validity of replacement tokens, potentially leading to broken authentication or unauthorized access.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is generic boilerplate — it restates the general best practice that tokens should be validated before storage, without identifying a specific exploitable vulnerability. The tokens are Personal Access Tokens for git repos (GitHub/GitLab); validating them at save time would require an extra API call to the git provider, which is not a standard requirement. Invalid tokens simply cause sync failures with clear error messages. Only admins can call this endpoint. The finding could be copy-pasted onto any credential-storing endpoint in any codebase without modification.
findings.severity_justification: Invalid tokens cause catalog sync failures with visible errors, not silent security bypasses. Only admins can configure catalog URLs and tokens.
findings.category_justification: The finding is framed as a potential authentication or authorization concern.

findings.message: The resolveToken implementation uses GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN as a fallback only for the default catalog URL. However, unauthorized usage of this token in other contexts could lead to security issues if attackers mimic this URL.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code explicitly addresses this concern in its own comment ('preventing the server-level token from leaking to attacker-controlled endpoints'). The catalogURL comes from admin-controlled spec fields — only admins can configure catalog source URLs. An attacker 'mimicking the URL' requires admin access, which already grants full system control. The finding restates a concern the code already handles without demonstrating a concrete exploit path.
findings.severity_justification: No exploitable path exists for non-admin attackers to control the catalogURL parameter and extract GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about potential token leakage to attacker-controlled endpoints.

findings.message: The isGitRepoURL function assumes a '.git' suffix or known domain to classify valid repositories but may misclassify URLs from unknown hosting platforms or corner cases, potentially leading to incorrect processing or security bypass.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is generic boilerplate about URL classification heuristics without identifying a specific misclassification or exploitable security bypass. The isGitRepoURL function is used to decide whether to treat a URL as a git repo (clone it) vs. a raw file (fetch it directly). Both code paths are safe — the wrong classification causes a functional error (clone failure or unexpected file fetch), not a security bypass. Only admins can configure catalog source URLs. The finding doesn't demonstrate any concrete problematic URL or exploit path.
findings.severity_justification: Misclassification of a URL would cause a sync error visible to the admin, not a security issue or silent data corruption. Admin-only configuration limits the attack surface.
findings.category_justification: The finding is framed as a potential security bypass.

findings.message: The GitLab API check for repository size only skips validation when a token is unavailable, which could lead to incomplete or inefficient handling if tokens are misconfigured or expired.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code already explicitly handles token-unavailable (empty), 401, and 403 responses by falling back to the clone-time sizeLimitedFS check. Expired tokens return 401 which is already handled. The pre-clone API check is an optimization; the sizeLimitedFS is the actual enforcement mechanism. The finding doesn't identify a specific unhandled case.
findings.severity_justification: No unhandled failure path exists; the clone-time size check acts as the fallback in all cases the finding describes.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about handling of token failures in a pre-clone size check.

findings.message: Move this to the direct dependency block.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The PR already moved github.com/go-git/go-billy/v5 from the indirect block to the direct dependencies block. At the current SHA, go-billy appears at line 26 in the direct requires block. The finding's suggested action was already implemented by this PR.
findings.severity_justification: The claimed issue doesn't exist at the reviewed SHA.
findings.category_justification: go.mod dependency classification.

findings.message: I know there are other places where we've used the UID as part of the credential context, but we should do that anymore. There are issues with doing that around migration and cleanup. Using the name of the catalog should be enough.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The new code at lines 153, 204, and 213 already uses catalog.Name (not UID) as the credential context — exactly what the finding says should be done. The finding affirms the implementation choice rather than identifying a bug. The concern about other places in the codebase using UID is a pre-existing issue unrelated to this PR's changes.
findings.severity_justification: No bug or incorrect behavior — the finding approves the current implementation.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about credential context naming convention and codebase consistency.

findings.message:
nit: you don't need the variable.
```suggestion
		if err != nil && !errors.As(err, & gptscript.ErrNotFound{}) {
```
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code in mcpcatalogs.go already uses the inline form errors.As(err, &gptscript.ErrNotFound{}) without an intermediate variable, consistent with the rest of the codebase. The finding's suggested replacement is identical to what is already written. No variable to remove.
findings.severity_justification: Even if applicable, this is a trivial style nit with no behavioral impact.
findings.category_justification: Nit about removing an unnecessary intermediate variable in an error check.

findings.message: I have received pushback previously in including clients in the "convert" functions. I was told that these should just take everything they need and shouldn't error unless absolutely necessary.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The convertMCPCatalog function already follows the described convention: it takes pre-fetched tokenEnv as a plain map (no client, no error return). The finding is a reviewer citing a project convention that the new code already correctly adheres to, not identifying a violation.
findings.severity_justification: No bug or convention violation present in the code.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about adherence to a project convention for convert functions.

findings.message: The logic from here down all seems very complicated. I believe this can be simplified if we have one credential with multiple keys in the `Env` map (one per URL). The determining old url, new url is simpler because you are only dealing with one credential.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code already implements a single credential with multiple Env keys (one per URL) via CatalogCredentialToolName = 'catalog-source-tokens'. newTokens is a map[string]string passed as the Env field of one credential. The finding's suggested approach is already what's implemented. The remaining complexity is inherent to the merge logic, not the storage format.
findings.severity_justification: No bug identified; the finding misreads the existing implementation.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about code complexity and design simplification.

findings.message: There are a lot of changes in this function that amount to no functionality change. Best practice is to make exactly the changes you need for your fix or feature.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The diff shows removal of several inline comments ('// Create request', '// Add authentication if token is available', '// Make the request', '// Check response status', '// Parse response') and minor error message rewording in checkGitHubRepoSize that are purely cosmetic and unrelated to the PR's functionality. These are bundled with legitimate functional changes, making the diff noisier than necessary.
findings.severity_justification: Cosmetic diff noise doesn't affect functionality or correctness, but it violates the project's stated best practice of minimal diffs and makes code review harder.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about keeping diffs focused on the actual feature change rather than mixing in cosmetic cleanups.

findings.message: Do we need this limited FS if we are also checking the size of the repo via the APIs?
findings.tp_fp_justification: The sizeLimitedFS is the only size enforcement for self-hosted repos (no API check in the switch statement) and GitLab repos without a token (checkGitLabRepoSize returns nil when token is empty). Removing it would leave these cases unprotected. The code comment already explains its role as a fallback. The finding asks a valid design question but the answer clearly supports keeping the implementation.
findings.severity_justification: The finding questions a design decision where the correct answer is to keep the existing code, so no action is warranted.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about defense-in-depth for repository size enforcement.

findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding references variables 'existingTokens' and 'existedCred' that don't exist in the code at this SHA. The code already uses existingCred.Env directly (e.g., existingCred.Env[u]) without an intermediate copy. The finding appears to have been generated against a different version of the code.
findings.severity_justification: The claimed issue doesn't exist in the code at the reviewed SHA.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about eliminating an unnecessary variable copy.

findings.message: Seems like this can be removed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: CatalogCredentialToolName is actively used in 5 places across 2 packages (mcpcatalog.go line 63, mcpcatalogs.go lines 153/205/213/1526). It's an exported cross-package constant that cannot be removed without breaking the build or inlining the string literal in all callers. The finding is factually incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: The claimed issue doesn't exist — the constant is in active use.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about whether a constant definition is necessary.

findings.message: In `List`, `revealCatalogTokens` is called once per catalog inside the loop, each issuing a separate `RevealCredential` round-trip to the gptscript credential store. For installations with many catalogs this turns a single list call into an N+1 credential-store fetch pattern. Consider batching or skipping the reveal when only presence (not the env contents) is needed for masking — the masked map could potentially be derived from a cheaper existence check.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is factually correct: revealCatalogTokens is called inside the for loop over list.Items, issuing one RevealCredential RPC per catalog. The call retrieves full credential env data when only key presence is needed for masking. The pattern was introduced by this PR.
findings.severity_justification: In practice there appears to be only one catalog (the Update handler enforces this), so the N+1 pattern has negligible real-world impact. It's a legitimate concern but unlikely to matter in any deployed instance.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about an N+1 RPC pattern where a single list call becomes multiple round-trips to the credential store.

findings.message: The `parseGitURL` doc-comment block is inconsistent: there is a stale leading comment ("readGitCatalog clones a git repository... It works with any git hosting platform...") immediately above `parseGitURL`, which is actually the documentation that belongs on `readGitCatalog` further down. As written the comments for the two functions are intermixed and misleading. Consider splitting the comment block so each function only has its own doc-comment.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Lines 211-218 show a comment block immediately preceding `parseGitURL` that starts with 'readGitCatalog clones a git repository over HTTPS and reads its catalog entries. It works with any git hosting platform...' followed by 'parseGitURL parses a git repository URL...' — two distinct functions' doc-comments are merged above the wrong function, making the Go doc for `parseGitURL` misleading and leaving `readGitCatalog` undocumented.
findings.severity_justification: This is a documentation/comment issue with no runtime impact. It's confusing for readers using `go doc` or IDEs, but doesn't affect correctness or behavior.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about a malformed doc-comment that conflates documentation for two different functions.

findings.message: The credential map is persisted with the raw source URL as the Env key and the catalog name as context, but the PR describes storing tokens under catalog UID + URL hash. Besides leaking private repository URLs into credential metadata, using the raw URL key is what prevents safe credential transfer when a source URL is edited.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The credential transfer on URL edit is provably broken: the frontend sends sourceURLCredentials[newUrl]='*', but the backend looks for existingCred.Env[newUrl] which was stored under the old URL key — causing the token to be silently dropped. The finding also correctly notes the PR description ('catalog UID + URL hash') doesn't match the implementation (catalog.Name + raw URL as Env keys).
findings.severity_justification: Editing a source URL with a stored token silently loses the token, requiring admins to re-enter PATs. This is a user-visible functional regression for a feature just introduced by this PR, though not a data-integrity or security issue.
findings.category_justification: The core issue is a logic bug: the '*' keep-existing-token path fails when a URL is renamed because it looks up a key that doesn't exist in the credential store.

findings.message: Credential-store failures are swallowed and converted to an empty token, so sync proceeds as an unauthenticated clone/fetch and reports a misleading git/raw catalog error instead of the real credential-store problem. Returning the error here would make private repo sync failures actionable and avoid unauthenticated fallback after a storage outage.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: revealCatalogCredential swallows non-NotFound credential-store errors and returns '' — the error is only logged, not recorded in mcpCatalog.Status.SyncErrors. Sync proceeds unauthenticated; for private repos the downstream git error surfaces in SyncErrors instead of the real cause. The code comment claiming failures are 'visible in the sync status' is incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: For private repos the clone fails anyway with a git auth error, so sync is not silently corrupted — it just reports a misleading error. For public repos the fallback to unauthenticated is harmless. The main impact is poor observability/debuggability rather than silent data loss.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about error handling and observability: a credential-store failure is masked, making operational diagnosis of sync failures harder.
